newsitem.title: UK: Major to hold out against single currency - paper.
newsitem.headline: Major to hold out against single currency - paper.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major has concluded it would be against Britain's interests to join a single European currency in the next five years, a British newspaper said on Monday.

Major was now seeking to persuade his finance minister Kenneth Clarke to agree to ditch the present "wait and see" policy in time for the general election which must be called by next May, the Daily Telegraph said.
The prime minister was understood to have received the backing of 18 of his 22-member cabinet for a policy shift to fight the election on a pledge to retain Britain's own sterling currency.

But he had yet to overcome the formidable opposition of Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke, who will be in Brussels on Monday for a meeting of European Union finance ministers planning the final stages of monetary union in 1999.

Although Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine on Sunday stressed the current platform that "discussions are going on about what a single currency regime will look like if it happens", the Telegraph said Major was keen to abandon the existing policy in the run-up to a general election.

"After months of battling with Tory (Conservative) Euro-sceptics to keep open his options, the prime minister has come to the view that Britain should not be part of the first wave signing up for a single currency," the Telegraph said.
The paper said almost two thirds of rank-and-file Conservative members of parliament contesting the next election would issue personal manifestos stating their opposition to a single currency.
In a Conservative Party deeply split over Europe, Clarke is the most pro-European member of Major's cabinet.

His stance towards Brussels has made him deeply unpopular with the right-wing of the party who believe only his opposition has stopped Major from ruling out taking Britain into an EU single currency in the next parliament.

European Commission President Jacques Santer meanwhile was quoted as saying big business and financial interests in Britain would create irresistible pressure for the country to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Santer said no British government, whether Conservative or Labour, would be able to resist such pressure.
In an interview with the Financial Times, Santer warned Britain against marginalising itself in Europe, saying: "Britain must be at the heart of Europe, playing a leading role."
Santer said EMU would definitely go ahead as planned in 1999 and, asked to look ahead to the year 2003, he said: "There will be monetary union and Britain will be a member."
